claim: Murine tendon-to-bone attachment cells are bi-fated, activating a mixture of chondrocyte and tenocyte transcriptomes.
source: Here, we show that murine tendon-to-bone attachment cells are bi-fated, activating a mixture of chondrocyte and tenocyte transcriptomes, under regulation of shared regulatory elements and Krüppel-like factors (KLFs) transcription factors.
evidence: Supported by bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data showing expression of both chondrogenic and tenogenic genes in attachment cells, validated by in situ hybridization.

claim: Attachment cells are regulated by shared regulatory elements and Krüppel-like factors (KLFs) transcription factors.
source: Here, we show that murine tendon-to-bone attachment cells are bi-fated, activating a mixture of chondrocyte and tenocyte transcriptomes, under regulation of shared regulatory elements and Krüppel-like factors (KLFs) transcription factors.
evidence: Supported by ATAC sequencing showing shared accessible chromatin areas, enhancer reporter assays, and functional studies blocking Klf2 and Klf4 expression.

claim: High-throughput bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing of humeral attachment cells revealed expression of hundreds of chondrogenic and tenogenic genes.
source: High-throughput bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing of humeral attachment cells revealed expression of hundreds of chondrogenic and tenogenic genes, which was validated by in situ hybridization and single-molecule ISH.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the RNA sequencing experiments performed in the study.

claim: ATAC sequencing showed that attachment cells share accessible intergenic chromatin areas with either tenocytes or chondrocytes.
source: ATAC sequencing showed that attachment cells share accessible intergenic chromatin areas with either tenocytes or chondrocytes.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq experiments performed in the study.

claim: Epigenomic analysis revealed enhancer signatures for most of the shared accessible intergenic chromatin regions.
source: Epigenomic analysis revealed enhancer signatures for most of these regions.
evidence: Based on computational intersection with ENCODE datasets of histone modification marks associated with enhancers.

claim: Transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays verified the shared activity of some enhancers.
source: Transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays verified the shared activity of some of these enhancers.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of in vivo enhancer reporter assays performed in the study.

claim: Integrative chromatin and motif analyses and transcriptomic data implicated KLFs as regulators of attachment cells.
source: Finally, integrative chromatin and motif analyses and transcriptomic data implicated KLFs as regulators of attachment cells.
evidence: Based on bioinformatic analysis of ATAC-seq peaks for transcription factor binding sites combined with transcriptomic data.

claim: Blocking expression of both Klf2 and Klf4 in developing limb mesenchyme impaired attachment cell differentiation.
source: Indeed, blocking expression of both Klf2 and Klf4 in developing limb mesenchyme impaired their differentiation.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of genetic knockout experiments using Prx1-Cre to delete Klf2 and Klf4.

claim: Elastic tendons have a Young's modulus in the order of 200 megapascal.
source: In the musculoskeleton, elastic tendons, which have a Young's modulus (a measure of stiffness) in the order of 200 megapascal, are attached to the much harder bone, with a modulus in the order of 20 gigapascal.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the mechanical properties of tendons.

claim: Bone has a Young's modulus in the order of 20 gigapascal.
source: In the musculoskeleton, elastic tendons, which have a Young's modulus (a measure of stiffness) in the order of 200 megapascal, are attached to the much harder bone, with a modulus in the order of 20 gigapascal.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the mechanical properties of bone.

claim: The enthesis is a transitional tissue that displays a gradual shift in cellular and extracellular properties from the tendon side through to the bone side.
source: The evolutionary solution to this problem is the enthesis, a transitional tissue that displays a gradual shift in cellular and extracellular properties from the tendon side through to the bone side (Genin et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012a; Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013; Thomopoulos et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on enthesis structure and function.

claim: Progenitors of the attachment unit express both Sox9 and scleraxis (Scx).
source: These studies identified the progenitors of the AU and showed that they express both the chondrogenic and tenogenic transcription factors Sox9 and scleraxis (Scx), respectively (Blitz et al., 2013; Sugimoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies that identified these progenitors.

claim: Sox9+/Scx+ progenitors differentiate to chondrocytes, which form a bone eminence on one side, or to tenocytes, which form the tendon on the other side.
source: Next, Sox9+/Scx+ progenitors differentiate to chondrocytes, which form a bone eminence on one side, or to tenocytes, which form the tendon on the other side, whereas the cells in between differentiate into Gli1+ cells that eventually will form the enthesis (Felsenthal et al., 2018; Schwartz et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on attachment unit development.

claim: Cells in between chondrocytes and tenocytes differentiate into Gli1+ cells that eventually will form the enthesis.
source: Next, Sox9+/Scx+ progenitors differentiate to chondrocytes, which form a bone eminence on one side, or to tenocytes, which form the tendon on the other side, whereas the cells in between differentiate into Gli1+ cells that eventually will form the enthesis (Felsenthal et al., 2018; Schwartz et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on attachment unit development.

claim: TGFβ signaling regulates the specification of attachment unit progenitors.
source: TGFβ signaling regulates the specification of AU progenitors, whereas BMP and FGF signaling as well as mechanical signals determine their fate and differentiation (Blitz et al., 2013; Blitz et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on signaling pathways in attachment unit development.

claim: BMP and FGF signaling as well as mechanical signals determine the fate and differentiation of attachment unit progenitors.
source: TGFβ signaling regulates the specification of AU progenitors, whereas BMP and FGF signaling as well as mechanical signals determine their fate and differentiation (Blitz et al., 2013; Blitz et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on signaling pathways in attachment unit development.

claim: Postnatal enthesis cells have been termed fibrocartilage cells based on their histological appearance.
source: Postnatal enthesis cells have been termed fibrocartilage cells based on their histological appearance, because they display morphological features that are shared with tenocytes and chondrocytes (Thomopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on enthesis cell morphology.

claim: Enthesis cells express collagens type I, II, and X; Indian hedgehog (Ihh); parathyroid hormone-related peptide (Pthlh); patched 1 (Ptc1); runt-related transcription factor 2 (Runx2); tenascin C (Tnc); and biglycan (Bgn).
source: In recent years, several studies have identified some of the genes that these cells express, including collagens type I, II, and X; Indian hedgehog (Ihh); parathyroid hormone-related peptide (Pthlh); patched 1 (Ptc1); runt-related transcription factor 2 (Runx2); tenascin C (Tnc); and biglycan (Bgn) (Liu et al., 2012b; Liu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2018; Thomopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies identifying genes expressed in enthesis cells.

claim: The fluorescent reporters tdTomato and GFP failed to label the attachment cells located between Col2a1-expressing chondrocytes and Scx-expressing tenocytes.
source: Unexpectedly, the two reporters failed to label the attachment cells that were located in between these two populations.
evidence: Directly observed in the Col2a1-Cre-tdTomato-Scx-GFP transgenic mice.

claim: The borders between tendon and attachment cells and between cartilage and attachment cells were clearly demarcated.
source: Nevertheless, the borders between tendon and attachment cells and between cartilage and attachment cells were clearly demarcated (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Directly observed in fluorescent imaging of transgenic mice.

claim: Principal components analysis showed that the transcriptomes of tenocytes and chondrocytes were clearly separated, whereas attachment cells were located between the two cell types.
source: Initial analysis of the different transcriptomes using principal components analysis (PCA) showed that the transcriptomes of tenocytes and chondrocytes were clearly separated, whereas attachment cells were located between the two cell types, recapitulating their anatomical positions.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of PCA analysis of bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: The attachment cell transcriptome is shared with both chondrocytes and tenocytes.
source: This suggests that the attachment cell transcriptome is shared with both chondrocytes and tenocytes (Figure 1B, PC1 31.66%).
evidence: Inferred from PCA analysis showing attachment cells positioned between tenocytes and chondrocytes.

claim: 374 genes exhibited differential expression between tenocytes and chondrocytes and were also expressed by attachment cells.
source: From these two clusters, 374 genes, 320 of them tenogenic and 54 chondrogenic, were also found to be expressed by attachment cells.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of clustering analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: 320 tenogenic genes were expressed by attachment cells.
source: From these two clusters, 374 genes, 320 of them tenogenic and 54 chondrogenic, were also found to be expressed by attachment cells.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of clustering analysis.

claim: 54 chondrogenic genes were expressed by attachment cells.
source: From these two clusters, 374 genes, 320 of them tenogenic and 54 chondrogenic, were also found to be expressed by attachment cells.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of clustering analysis.

claim: Attachment cells express Sox9, Col2a1, and Acan (chondrogenic markers).
source: They included major regulators and marker genes of the two tissues, such as Sox9, Col2a1, and Acan for chondrocytes and Col1a1, Col1a2, Scx, and Col5a1 for tenocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of transcriptomic analysis and shown in heatmap.

claim: Attachment cells express Col1a1, Col1a2, Scx, and Col5a1 (tenogenic markers).
source: They included major regulators and marker genes of the two tissues, such as Sox9, Col2a1, and Acan for chondrocytes and Col1a1, Col1a2, Scx, and Col5a1 for tenocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of transcriptomic analysis and shown in heatmap.

claim: 54 genes were found to be upregulated in cartilage adjacent to attachment cells alone.
source: The third cluster comprised 54 genes that were found to be upregulated in cartilage adjacent to attachment cells alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of clustering analysis.

claim: 23 genes were found to be uniquely upregulated in attachment cells.
source: our analysis identified 24 and 23 genes that were found to be down- or upregulated in attachment cells, shown by the fourth and fifth clusters, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of clustering analysis.

claim: Genes uniquely upregulated in attachment cells include transcription factors such as Krüppel-like factors (KLFs), Lmo1, and Gli1.
source: The genes that were found to be uniquely upregulated in attachment cells included transcription factors, such as the Krüppel-like factors (KLFs), Lmo1, and Gli1, which could act as regulators of the genetic program of attachment cells.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of analysis of cluster 5 genes.

claim: Hierarchical clustering showed that attachment cells are closer to tenocytes than to chondrocytes.
source: To determine the relative proximity of attachment cells to the other two cell types, we performed hierarchical clustering on the 865 differentially expressed genes. Results showed that these cells are closer to tenocytes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: Double-fluorescent in situ hybridization showed that tenogenic and chondrogenic markers were co-expressed by attachment cells.
source: As seen in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4, in agreement with the transcriptome analysis, the selected markers were co-expressed by the attachment cells.
evidence: Directly observed in double-FISH experiments.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq of E13.5 Sox9+/Scx+ attachment progenitors revealed five transcriptionally distinct subpopulations.
source: Results showed five transcriptionally distinct subpopulations (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Clusters 1 and 3 of attachment progenitors were highly rich with chondrogenic genes (Sox9, Sox5, Col2a1, Wwp2).
source: Examination of the top-10 differentially expressed genes across clusters revealed that they were subdivided to three main categories. Clusters 1 and 3 were highly rich with chondrogenic genes (Sox9, Sox5, Col2a1, Wwp2), whereas clusters 2 and 4 were highly rich with tenogenic genes (Scx, Hic1, Ptn, Igfbp5).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of scRNA-seq cluster analysis.

claim: Clusters 2 and 4 of attachment progenitors were highly rich with tenogenic genes (Scx, Hic1, Ptn, Igfbp5).
source: Examination of the top-10 differentially expressed genes across clusters revealed that they were subdivided to three main categories. Clusters 1 and 3 were highly rich with chondrogenic genes (Sox9, Sox5, Col2a1, Wwp2), whereas clusters 2 and 4 were highly rich with tenogenic genes (Scx, Hic1, Ptn, Igfbp5).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of scRNA-seq cluster analysis.

claim: Cluster 0 of attachment progenitors was highly rich with genes such as Col1a1, Alpl, Spp1, Runx2, Bicc1, Maf, and Mef2c.
source: By contrast, the identity of cluster 0 was less specified, as it was highly rich with genes such as Col1a1, Alpl, Spp1, and Runx2 in addition to Bicc1, Maf, and Mef2c (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of scRNA-seq cluster analysis.

claim: All five clusters of attachment progenitors contained both chondrogenic and tenogenic marker genes.
source: As seen in Figure 2B, all five clusters contained both chondrogenic and tenogenic marker genes.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of scRNA-seq analysis and shown in violin plots.

claim: Single-molecule FISH confirmed that Wwp2 and Bgn were co-expressed in attachment cells at a single-cell resolution.
source: As seen and quantified in Figure 2C,D, Wwp2 and Bgn were indeed co-expressed in the attachment cells.
evidence: Directly observed in smFISH experiments.

claim: Attachment cells express in parallel both chondrogenic and tenogenic genes.
source: Overall, these results indicate that attachment cells are bi-fated, expressing in parallel both chondrogenic and tenogenic genes (referred to in the following as mixed transcriptome or mixed expression profile).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from bulk RNA-seq, scRNA-seq, and smFISH data.

claim: PCA analysis of accessible chromatin profiles revealed that tenocytes and chondrocytes were clearly separated, while attachment cells resided between these two cell types.
source: Initial PCA analysis of accessible chromatin profiles for each FACS-sorted cell population once again revealed that tenocytes and chondrocytes were clearly separated, while attachment cells resided between these two cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of PCA analysis of ATAC-seq data.

claim: Attachment cells had a significantly lower number of unique ATAC-seq peaks compared to tenocytes and chondrocytes.
source: While the majority of the peaks were shared by all three cell types, attachment cells had a significantly lower number of unique peaks (p<1e-4 relative to both cell types, chi-square with Yates correction), and a significantly higher overlap with the other two cell types (p<2.2e-1).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of statistical analysis of ATAC-seq peak overlap.

claim: Attachment cells had a significantly higher overlap of ATAC-seq peaks with tenocytes and chondrocytes.
source: While the majority of the peaks were shared by all three cell types, attachment cells had a significantly lower number of unique peaks (p<1e-4 relative to both cell types, chi-square with Yates correction), and a significantly higher overlap with the other two cell types (p<2.2e-1).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of statistical analysis of ATAC-seq peak overlap.

claim: 13,017 ATAC-seq peaks were located near transcription start sites (TSSs).
source: Analysis of the ATAC-seq signal revealed that 13,017 peaks were located near transcription start sites (TSSs), whereas 31,856 peaks were in intergenic or intron regions.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak annotation.

claim: 31,856 ATAC-seq peaks were in intergenic or intron regions.
source: Analysis of the ATAC-seq signal revealed that 13,017 peaks were located near transcription start sites (TSSs), whereas 31,856 peaks were in intergenic or intron regions.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak annotation.

claim: 87% of TSS peaks were accessible in all three cell types (tenocytes, attachment cells, and chondrocytes).
source: Most of the peaks that were located near TSSs were accessible in all three cell types (87%), and only 13% were accessible in one or two cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak analysis.

claim: 13% of TSS peaks were accessible in only one or two cell types.
source: Most of the peaks that were located near TSSs were accessible in all three cell types (87%), and only 13% were accessible in one or two cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak analysis.

claim: 86% of TSS peaks associated with differentially expressed genes were accessible in all three cell types.
source: We found that 819 peaks were located near transcription start sites (TSSs), whereas 2340 peaks were in intergenic or intron regions. Most of the peaks that were located near TSSs (708, 86%) were accessible in all three cell types, and only 111 (13%) were accessible in one or two cell types (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: 74.7% of intergenic peaks associated with differentially expressed genes were specific to one or two cell types.
source: Interestingly, a significantly higher fraction of intergenic peaks were specific to one or two cell types (1767, 74.7%, p=0, chi-square test, Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of statistical analysis of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 920 intergenic peaks were accessible in attachment cells.
source: Out of these 1767 intergenic peaks, 920 peaks were accessible in attachment cell; 672 were shared with either tenocytes or chondrocytes; and 248 were accessible only in attachment cells (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak analysis.

claim: 672 intergenic peaks accessible in attachment cells were shared with either tenocytes or chondrocytes.
source: Out of these 1767 intergenic peaks, 920 peaks were accessible in attachment cell; 672 were shared with either tenocytes or chondrocytes; and 248 were accessible only in attachment cells (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak analysis.

claim: 248 intergenic peaks were accessible only in attachment cells.
source: Out of these 1767 intergenic peaks, 920 peaks were accessible in attachment cell; 672 were shared with either tenocytes or chondrocytes; and 248 were accessible only in attachment cells (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of ATAC-seq peak analysis.

claim: The 920 intergenic elements accessible in attachment cells may act as enhancers that drive the transcriptome of these cells.
source: These results suggest that the 920 intergenic elements that were accessible in attachment cells may act as enhancers that drive the transcriptome of these cells.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq data showing accessible intergenic regions in attachment cells.

claim: A region at −42 kb from the TSS of Mgp was accessible in chondrocytes and attachment cells, but not in tenocytes.
source: For example, as shown in Figure 3D, we identified a region at −42 kb from the TSS of Mgp, a bona fide chondrogenic marker (Barone et al., 1991), which was accessible in chondrocytes and attachment cells, whereas in tenocytes this site was closed.
evidence: Directly observed in ATAC-seq data visualization.

claim: A region at +303 kb from Sox9 was accessible in attachment cells and chondrocytes, but not in tenocytes.
source: Another example is Sox9, a bona fide chondrogenic marker. At +303 kb from Sox9, we identified a region that was accessible in attachment cells and chondrocytes, but not in tenocytes.
evidence: Directly observed in ATAC-seq data visualization.

claim: A region at −330 kb from the TSS of Col11a1 was accessible in attachment cells and chondrocytes, but not in tenocytes.
source: The same pattern was observed for a region at −330 kb from the TSS of a third bona fide chondrogenic marker, namely Col11a1 (Li et al., 1995).
evidence: Directly observed in ATAC-seq data visualization.

claim: A region at −17 kb from the TSS of Col1a2 was accessible in attachment cells and tenocytes, but not in chondrocytes.
source: The opposite pattern was observed at −17 kb from the TSS of Col1a2, a bona fide tenogenic marker, where we identified a region that was accessible in attachment cells and tenocytes, but not in chondrocytes.
evidence: Directly observed in ATAC-seq data visualization.

claim: The mechanism for the activation of a mixed transcriptome in attachment cells is based on sharing regulatory elements with chondrocytes or tenocytes.
source: This suggests that the mechanism for the activation of a mixed transcriptome in attachment cells is based on sharing regulatory elements with chondrocytes or tenocytes.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq data showing shared accessible chromatin regions.

claim: Five enhancer elements were found to be active in mouse forelimbs at E14.5.
source: Five elements were found to be active in the mouse forelimbs, as well as in other anatomical areas (Figure 4).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays.

claim: The Col1a1-associated element drove lacZ expression at the teres major insertion into the scapula.
source: The Col1a1-associated element drove lacZ expression at the teres major insertion into the scapula, in agreement with the ATAC-seq results, which predicted its activity in tenocytes and attachment cells (n = 2/9).
evidence: Directly observed in transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays.

claim: The Klf2 element drove reporter activity in hypertrophic chondrocytes and perichondrium at the humerus and forelimb digits.
source: The Klf2 element indeed drove reporter activity in hypertrophic chondrocytes and perichondrium at the humerus and forelimb digits, in addition to the skull and mandible (Figure 4, n = 3/3).
evidence: Directly observed in transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays.

claim: The Sox9 element showed activity solely in hypertrophic chondrocytes of the humerus.
source: The Sox9 element showed activity solely in hypertrophic chondrocytes of the humerus (n = 4/7).
evidence: Directly observed in transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays.

claim: The Mgp element showed activity in forelimb and hindlimb, specifically in hip, metacarpal joints and digits as well as in the posterior distal side of the femur.
source: Its activity was seen in forelimb and hindlimb, specifically in hip, metacarpal joints and digits as well as in the posterior distal side of the femur, a site where ligaments (e.g. the cruciate ligaments) are inserted into the femur at the knee area and at ligament insertion into to the hip (e.g. iliofemoral ligament; Figure 4, n = 3/3), verifying its activity in chondrocytes and attachment cells.
evidence: Directly observed in transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays.

claim: The Col11a1 element showed activity in the greater tuberosity insertion, as well as in the posterior side of the skull, the nasal bone area and the anterior distal side of the femur.
source: Its activity verified the bioinformatic analysis, showing LacZ staining in the greater tuberosity insertion, as well as in the posterior side of the skull, the nasal bone area and the anterior distal side of the femur (Figure 4, n = 11/11).
evidence: Directly observed in transgenic mouse enhancer reporter assays.

claim: Shared enhancers activate a mixed transcriptome in attachment cells.
source: Overall, these results provide a proof of concept for the ability of the accessible intergenic elements we have identified to act as enhancers that drive expression in both attachment cells and chondrocytes or tenocytes. This supports our hypothesis that shared enhancers activate a mixed transcriptome in attachment cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from enhancer reporter assay results combined with ATAC-seq data.

claim: Genomatix analysis identified NFIs (Nfia), GLIs (Gli1), KLFs (Klf2 and Klf4), ZBTBs (Zbtb48) and RUNXs (Runx3) as differentially expressed transcription factors in attachment cells.
source: Among the differentially expressed genes at E14.5 we identified NFIs (Nfia), GLIs (Gli1), KLFs (Klf2 and Klf4), ZBTBs (Zbtb48) and RUNXs (Runx3; Table 2, Figure 5A), whose expression was upregulated in attachment cells.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of Genomatix analysis of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: HOMER motif analysis showed significant over-representation of KLFs and RUNXs transcription factor binding sites.
source: Further support for these results was provided by HOMER motif analysis (Heinz et al., 2010), which showed significant over-representation of KLFs and RUNXs TFBSs.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of HOMER motif analysis.

claim: In situ hybridization validated that Klf2 is expressed in attachment cells at E14.5.
source: Focusing on Klf2, which was found to be differentially expressed by the bulk transcriptome analysis of the attachment site (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), we first validated its expression in the forming attachment site by ISH (Figure 5B).
evidence: Directly observed in ISH experiments.

claim: Three enhancers shown to be active in attachment cells had Klf2-binding sites in their sequence.
source: Next, we analyzed the enhancers that were shown by the bioinformatic analysis to be active in attachment cells and either tenocytes or chondrocytes (Figure 4). Three of these enhancers had Klf2-binding sites in their sequence (Table 1), further supporting a potential role for KLFs during attachment site development.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of bioinformatic analysis of enhancer sequences.

claim: KLF4 has ~90% sequence similarity to KLF2 in its zinc finger DNA-binding domain.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that Klf2 and Klf4 are functionally redundant, as KLF4 has ~90% sequence similarity to KLF2 in its zinc finger DNA-binding domain, suggesting that these factors could have common target sequences (Chiplunkar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on KLF protein similarity.

claim: Klf2 and Klf4 expression was found in Sox9+/Scx+ attachment progenitors by scRNA-seq analysis.
source: In our scRNA-seq analysis, the expression of both genes was found in Sox9+/Scx+ attachment progenitors (Figure 5C).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: In E15.5 control mice, attachment cells were packed together and surrounded by ECM.
source: Transverse histological sections through the deltoid tuberosity of E15.5 control mice showed that the attachment cells were packed together and surrounded by ECM (Figure 5Da').
evidence: Directly observed in histological sections.

claim: In E15.5 Prx1-Klf2-Klf4 dcKO embryos, the putative attachment site cells were sparse with reduced ECM.
source: In contrast, in the putative attachment site of Prx1-Klf2-Klf4 double conditional knockout (dcKO) embryos, the cells were sparse with reduced ECM (Figure 5Db').
evidence: Directly observed in histological sections.

claim: By E18.5, attachment cells failed to differentiate in Prx1-Klf2-Klf4 dcKO embryos.
source: By E18.5, this difference was more pronounced, as attachment cells failed to differentiate (Figure 5Dc',d').
evidence: Directly observed in histological sections.

claim: The expression of Col1a1, Gli1, Bsp, Bgn, and Col5a1 was reduced in the dcKO attachment site relative to the control.
source: Indeed, we found that the expression of Col1a1, Gli1, Bsp, Bgn, and Col5a1 was reduced in the dcKO attachment site, relative to the control (Figure 5De-p), supporting a role for KLF2/4 in attachment cells differentiation.
evidence: Directly observed in ISH experiments comparing control and dcKO embryos.

claim: 72% of the 374 attachment genes had KLF2/4 binding sites in their regulatory regions.
source: Interestingly, we found that many of these genes had KLF2/4 binding sites in their regulatory regions (72% of the 374 attachment genes relative to 53% in the whole genome, p<1e-4, chi-square).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of bioinformatic analysis of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Gli1 has KLF2/4 transcription factor binding sites in peaks that reside −2.1 and −1.5 kb from its TSS.
source: For Gli1, we found KLF2/4 TFBSs in peaks that reside −2.1 and −1.5 kb from its TSS (Table 3).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of bioinformatic analysis of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Col5a1 has multiple binding sites for KLF2 or KLF4.
source: For Col5a1, we found multiple binding sites for KLF2 or KLF4.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of bioinformatic analysis of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: KLF2/4 play an essential role in regulating attachment cell gene expression.
source: Together, these results indicate that KLF2/4 play an essential role in regulating attachment cell gene expression.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic knockout experiments and bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Over 30% of the population over the age of 60 will injure their shoulder's rotator cuff.
source: For example, over 30% of the population over the age of 60 will injure their shoulder's rotator cuff (Lehman et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on rotator cuff injuries.

claim: Failure rates of surgical reattachment range from 20% for small tears to 94% for repair of massive tears.
source: Failure rates of surgical reattachment range from 20% for small tears to 94% for repair of massive tears (Galatz et al., 2004; Harryman et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on surgical outcomes.

claim: Attachment cells display morphological features that are shared with tenocytes and chondrocytes.
source: These cells display morphological features that are shared with tenocytes and chondrocytes (Thomopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on attachment cell morphology.

claim: The finding of mixed matrix genes in the transcriptome of attachment cells may provide a mechanism for the formation of a transitional tissue.
source: Moreover, the finding of mixed matrix genes in the transcriptome of the attachment cells may provide a mechanism for the formation of a transitional tissue, which allows safe transfer of forces by the tendon between muscle and bone.
evidence: Inferred from transcriptomic data showing mixed gene expression.

claim: The heterogeneity revealed by scRNA-seq may represent the differentiation processes that Sox9/Scx-positive progenitors undergo during development.
source: This heterogeneity may represent the differentiation processes that the Sox9/Scx-positive progenitors undergo during development, ultimately leading to their terminal cell fate.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of scRNA-seq heterogeneity data.

claim: The high percentage of shared accessible intergenic sites between attachment cells and one group of flanking cells suggests this is the main mechanism for bi-fated state.
source: By contrast, the high percentage of shared accessible intergenic sites between attachment cells and one group of flanking cells, that is chondrocytes or tenocytes, suggests that this is the main mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq data showing shared accessible chromatin regions.

claim: Attachment-specific accessible elements may act as enhancers that drive the expression of genes specific to attachment cells.
source: These attachment-specific elements may act as enhancers that drive the expression of genes that are specific to attachment cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of ATAC-seq data showing attachment-specific peaks.

claim: During development, limb mesenchymal progenitors display highly accessible chromatin.
source: It is possible that during development, limb mesenchymal progenitors display highly accessible chromatin; yet, during differentiation, this accessibility is restricted to prevent the expression of genes from alternate lineages.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed chromatin accessibility patterns.

claim: In bi-fated attachment cells, shared accessible sites are maintained accessible to allow expression of the mixed transcriptome.
source: In contrast to this restriction process, in the bi-fated attachment cells the shared sites are maintained accessible to allow the expression of the mixed transcriptome.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed chromatin accessibility patterns in attachment cells.

claim: Polycomb-repressed chromatin leads to silencing of genes of alternate lineages, leading to commitment to a specific cell fate.
source: For example, polycomb-repressed chromatin leads to silencing of genes of alternate lineages, leading to the commitment to a specific cell fate (Aldiri et al., 2017; Laugesen and Helin, 2014; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on polycomb-mediated gene silencing.

claim: Deletion of Ezh2 in the developing limb leads to skeletal malformations.
source: Interestingly, previous studies demonstrated the importance of chromatin repression in the developing limb, showing how deletion of Ezh2, which acts as the enzymatically active subunit of PRC2, leads to skeletal malformations (Deimling et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on Ezh2 function in limb development.

claim: KLF2 and KLF4 regulate several biological processes including differentiation of gut and skin (KLF4) and the immune system (KLF2).
source: KLF2 and KLF4 are known to regulate several biological processes, such as promoting the differentiation of gut and skin (KLF4, [Katz et al., 2002; Segre et al., 1999]) as well as the immune system (KLF2, [Kuo et al., 1997]), maintaining pluripotency of embryonic stem cells (KLF2 and KLF4, [Jiang et al., 2008]), and, together with other factors, inducing pluripotency to generate iPSC by reprogramming (KLF4, [Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006]).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on KLF functions.

claim: KLF2 and KLF4 maintain pluripotency of embryonic stem cells.
source: KLF2 and KLF4 are known to regulate several biological processes, such as promoting the differentiation of gut and skin (KLF4, [Katz et al., 2002; Segre et al., 1999]) as well as the immune system (KLF2, [Kuo et al., 1997]), maintaining pluripotency of embryonic stem cells (KLF2 and KLF4, [Jiang et al., 2008]), and, together with other factors, inducing pluripotency to generate iPSC by reprogramming (KLF4, [Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006]).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on KLF functions in stem cells.

claim: KLF4, together with other factors, induces pluripotency to generate iPSC by reprogramming.
source: KLF2 and KLF4 are known to regulate several biological processes, such as promoting the differentiation of gut and skin (KLF4, [Katz et al., 2002; Segre et al., 1999]) as well as the immune system (KLF2, [Kuo et al., 1997]), maintaining pluripotency of embryonic stem cells (KLF2 and KLF4, [Jiang et al., 2008]), and, together with other factors, inducing pluripotency to generate iPSC by reprogramming (KLF4, [Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006]).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on iPSC generation.

claim: Klf4 over-expression in osteoblasts caused delayed bone development and impaired blood vessel invasion and osteoclast recruitment.
source: In bones, Klf4 over-expression in osteoblasts caused delayed bone development, in addition to impaired blood vessel invasion and osteoclast recruitment (Michikami et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on KLF4 function in bone.

claim: KLF2/4 are expressed during chick limb development in tendons and ligaments as part of the genetic program that regulates connective tissues.
source: Another study showed that KLF2/4 are expressed during chick limb development in tendons and ligaments as part of the genetic program that regulates connective tissues (Orgeur et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on KLF expression in connective tissues.

claim: Loss of both KLF2 and KLF4 during embryogenesis led to abnormal blood vessel development and early lethality.
source: Indeed, loss of both KLF2 and KLF4 during embryogenesis led to abnormal blood vessel development and early lethality. This phenotype was more severe than what was observed in embryos that lost only KLF2 or KLF4 (Chiplunkar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on KLF2/4 double knockout phenotype.

claim: 313 target genes are shared between KLF2 and KLF4.
source: Furthermore, previous work identified 313 target genes shared between KLF2 and KLf4, suggesting that they overlap in regulating gene expression (Orgeur et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on KLF2/4 target genes.

claim: While the attachment did form initially in the absence of KLF2/4, the subsequent differentiation failed.
source: While the attachment did form initially in their absence, the subsequent differentiation failed, suggesting that KLF2/4 play a role at this stage.
evidence: Directly observed in Prx1-Klf2-Klf4 dcKO embryos.

claim: KLF2/4 likely play a role in other musculoskeletal tissues such as the skeleton, tendon, and muscle.
source: While we concentrated in this study on the attachment site, it is most likely that KLF2/4 play a role also in other musculoskeletal tissues such as the skeleton, tendon, and muscle.
evidence: Speculative inference based on previous literature showing KLF2/4 expression in these tissues.

claim: Shear stress on vessels induced by blood flow leads to upregulation of Klf2 expression in mice.
source: It was shown in mice that shear stress on the vessels induced by blood flow leads to upregulation of Klf2 expression (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on mechanical regulation of Klf2.

claim: In vitro studies showed that KLF2 and KLF4 are influenced by shear stress.
source: Additional in vitro studies showed that KLF2 and KLF4 are influenced by shear stress (Chiplunkar et al., 2013; Dekker et al., 2005; Villarreal et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on mechanical regulation of KLF2/4.

claim: KLF2/4 may be regulated by muscle forces, leading to proper differentiation and maturation of the attachment site.
source: It is therefore possible that these factors are regulated by muscle forces, leading to the proper differentiation and maturation of the attachment site.
evidence: Speculative inference based on previous literature showing mechanical regulation of KLF2/4.

claim: Not all genes expressed by attachment cells have KLF2/4 binding sites in their regulatory regions, suggesting these two factors are part of a larger transcriptional network.
source: Yet, it is clear that not all of them share this property, suggesting that these two factors are part of a larger transcriptional network.
evidence: Inferred from bioinformatic analysis showing that not all attachment genes have KLF2/4 binding sites.

claim: Gli1 was previously reported as a marker for enthesis cells.
source: Gli1 was previously reported as a marker for enthesis cells (Dyment et al., 2015; Felsenthal et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012a; Schwartz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on Gli1 expression in enthesis.

claim: Loss of the tendon regulator Scx in mice led to failure of attachment cells to differentiate.
source: Indeed, loss of the tendon regulator Scx in mice led to failure of attachment cells to differentiate.
evidence: Supported by previous literature on Scx function in attachment development.

claim: Loss of the chondrogenic regulator Sox9 in Scx-expressing cells led to failure in attachment site formation.
source: Additionally, loss of the chondrogenic regulator Sox9 in Scx-expressing cells led to failure in attachment site formation (Blitz et al., 2013; Blitz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on Sox9 function in attachment development.

claim: The strategy of sharing enhancers allows the formation of a unique transitional tissue without developing de novo a dedicated genetic program.
source: This strategy allows the formation of a unique transitional tissue without developing de novo a dedicated genetic program that regulates a third, new cell fate.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the combined transcriptomic and epigenomic data.
